Part 1: Modelling Distance from the Center of the Drawing using ARIMA¶

Data Processing, Feature Engineering and EDA¶

In [2]:
# Select drawing
index = 56430 # Drawing was chosen 
seq = np.load("cat_56430.npy")
x = seq[:, 1]
y = seq[:, 2]

# Calculate distance from center (feature engineering)
# Center is defined as the (mean(x), mean(y))
center_x = np.mean(x)
center_y = np.mean(y)
distance_from_center = np.sqrt((x - center_x)**2 + (y - center_y)**2)

# Use sequence index as time (0, 1, 2, ...)
time_steps = np.arange(len(seq))

# Processed data: [sequence_index, x, y, distance_from_center]
# distance_from_center is the main focus of the project
# x and y will be used at the very end for a 2D VARIMA model and "forecast drift analysis"
processed_data = np.column_stack([time_steps, x, y, distance_from_center])

print(f"Processed data shape: {processed_data.shape}")
print(f"Columns: [sequence_index, x, y, distance_from_center]")

Columns: [sequence_index, x, y, distance_from_center]

In [5]:
# Plot chosen drawing and distance_from_center time plot
def plot_drawing_and_timeseries(time_steps, x, y, center_x, center_y, distance_from_center, index):
    """Plot drawing and its time series"""
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
    
    # Drawing
    axes[0].scatter(x, y, c='black', s=10, alpha=0.6)
    axes[0].scatter(center_x, center_y, color='red', s=100, marker='x', label='Center')
    axes[0].set_aspect('equal')
    axes[0].invert_yaxis()
    axes[0].set_title(f'Drawing #{index} ({len(x)} points)')
    axes[0].legend()
    axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    
    # Distance from center time series
    axes[1].plot(time_steps, distance_from_center, linewidth=2)
    axes[1].set_xlabel('Sequence Index')
    axes[1].set_ylabel('Distance from Center')
    axes[1].set_title('Time Series')
    axes[1].grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# Time plot shows that there is pattern for distance_from_center (i.e. not random noise)
plot_drawing_and_timeseries(time_steps, x, y, center_x, center_y, distance_from_center, index)

Comments

  • Time plot highlights both non-stationarity in variance and mean. This highlights a need for differencing and variance stabilizing transformation.
  • For completion, note that distance is positive (trivial).

Next Steps

  • Non-stationarity in variance would be handled first as differencing may result in negative values.

Handling non-stationarity in variance¶

In [6]:
# STEP 1: Finding the optimal transformation
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("Finding the optimal transformation".upper())
print("="*80)

transformations = {}

# Original
transformations['Original'] = distance_from_center

# Some common transformations for visualizing time plot
transformations['Square Root (λ=0.5)'] = np.sqrt(distance_from_center)
transformations['Cube Root (λ=0.33)'] = np.power(distance_from_center, 1/3)
transformations['Fourth Root (λ=0.25)'] = np.power(distance_from_center, 0.25)
transformations['Log (λ=0)'] = np.log(distance_from_center)
transformations['Square (λ=2)'] = np.power(distance_from_center, 2)

# Use Box-Cox's in-built optimiser to find the optimal lambda (last plot)
boxcox_data, lambda_boxcox = boxcox(distance_from_center)
transformations[f'Box-Cox (λ={lambda_boxcox:.3f})'] = boxcox_data
print(f"Box-Cox optimal λ: {lambda_boxcox:.4f}")

print(f"\nTotal transformations: {len(transformations)}")

# Step 2: Print the transformed time plot and distribution plot side by side
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("Transformed Time Plot and Distribution plot".upper())
print("="*80)

for name, data in transformations.items():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(18, 5))
    
    # Time series
    axes[0].plot(time_steps, data, linewidth=1.5)
    axes[0].set_title(f'{name}', fontsize=14)
    axes[0].set_xlabel('Sequence Index')
    axes[0].set_ylabel('Value')
    axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    
    # Distribution
    axes[1].hist(data, bins=50, edgecolor='black', alpha=0.7)
    axes[1].set_title(f'{name}', fontsize=14)
    axes[1].set_xlabel('Value')
    axes[1].set_ylabel('Frequency')
    axes[1].grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Check for non-stationarity in mean robustly¶

In [7]:
# Find nlags using sqrt of sample size 
nlags = (distance_from_center.shape[0]**0.5//1)

# Calculate ACF with confidence intervals
acf_vals, acf_confint = acf(distance_from_center, nlags=nlags, alpha=0.05)

# Visualize ACF plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
plot_acf(distance_from_center, lags=nlags, ax=axes, auto_ylims=True)
axes.set_title(f'SACF - Drawing #{index}')
axes.set_xlabel('Lag')
axes.set_ylabel('ACF')
plt.show()

Comments

  • ACF decays slowly. This indicates non-stationarity.

Next Steps

  • Therefore, model will be differenced.

Handling non-stationarity via differencing¶

Comments

  • Time plot
    • Centered around zero.
    • No trend.
    • There are occasional large spikes. Might have to investigated later. Probably caused by different strokes as the digital pen is lifted and placed elsewhere cause a change in velocity.
    • Indicates stationarity (mostly).
  • Distribution plot
    • Nothing unusual except for few outliers.
    • Since there are only a few outliers, they will be ignored.
    • Indicates stationarity (mostly).
  • ACF
    • Decays very fast.
    • Indicates no stationarity.
  • Conclusion
    • Non-stationarity has been fixed after one iteration of differencing.

Determing first model using ACF or PACF¶

In [10]:
# STEP 1: Calculate ACF & PACF with 95% confidence intervals
print(f"Using {nlags} lags for analysis\n")

acf_vals, acf_confint = acf(differenced_data, nlags=nlags, alpha=0.05)
pacf_vals, pacf_confint = pacf(differenced_data, nlags=nlags, alpha=0.05)


# STEP 2: Find significant lags (outside bounds)
# ACF
acf_significant_lags = []
for lag in range(len(acf_vals)):
    lower, upper = acf_confint[lag]
    if 0 < lower or 0 > upper:  # 0 is outside [lower, upper]
        acf_significant_lags.append(lag)
# Find PACF
pacf_significant_lags = []
for lag in range(len(pacf_vals)):
    lower, upper = pacf_confint[lag]
    if 0 < lower or 0 > upper:
        pacf_significant_lags.append(lag)

print("\n" + "="*80)
print("SIGNIFICANT LAGS")
print("="*80)
print("ACF - Significant Lags:")
print(f"  {acf_significant_lags}")
print(f"  Total: {len(acf_significant_lags)} out of {len(acf_vals)} lags\n")


# STEP 3: ACF and PACF plots
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("PLOTS")
print("="*80)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(18, 6))

# ACF Plot
plot_acf(differenced_data, lags=nlags, ax=axes[0])
for lag in acf_significant_lags:
    if lag <= nlags:
        axes[0].scatter(lag, acf_vals[lag], color='red', s=100, zorder=5, 
                       marker='o', edgecolors='darkred', linewidths=2)
axes[0].set_title(f'ACF - Differenced Data\n{len(acf_significant_lags)} Significant Lags (red circles)', 
                 fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Lag', fontsize=12)
axes[0].set_ylabel('ACF', fontsize=12)
axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# PACF Plot
plot_pacf(differenced_data, lags=nlags, ax=axes[1])
for lag in pacf_significant_lags:
    if lag <= nlags:
        axes[1].scatter(lag, pacf_vals[lag], color='red', s=100, zorder=5, 
                       marker='o', edgecolors='darkred', linewidths=2)
axes[1].set_title(f'PACF - Differenced Data\n{len(pacf_significant_lags)} Significant Lags (red circles)', 
                 fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Lag', fontsize=12)
axes[1].set_ylabel('PACF', fontsize=12)
axes[1].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Comments

  • Domain knowledge: Current time series uses differenced position. In drawing the next change in position is affected by the previous change in position. For example, if you are drawing a diagonal you are more likely to drag the cursor along that diagonal. Same applies to other shapes. Therefore, AR model is more suited.
  • Moreover, PACF has no later lags. Therefore, it requires no additional justification for borderline cases.
  • Given both these, PACF will be used to determine the next model.
  • The model chosen in AR(1).

Next Steps

  • Fit AR(1) model.
  • Fitted AR(1) model diagnostics.

# Create text summary
test_text = f"""
SHAPIRO-WILK TEST FOR NORMALITY
{'='*40}

H₀: Residuals are normally distributed
H₁: Residuals are NOT normally distributed

Test Statistic: {shapiro_stat:.6f}
P-value:        {shapiro_pvalue:.6f}

{'='*40}
"""

if shapiro_pvalue > 0.05:
    result_text = f"""
RESULT: ACCEPT H₀
(p-value = {shapiro_pvalue:.4f} > 0.05)

Residuals ARE normally distributed
AR(1) assumptions satisfied!
"""
    color = 'lightgreen'
else:
    result_text = f"""
RESULT: REJECT H₀
(p-value = {shapiro_pvalue:.4f} ≤ 0.05)

Residuals are NOT normally distributed
AR(1) assumptions violated!
"""
    color = 'lightcoral'

axes[1, 2].text(0.1, 0.9, test_text, transform=axes[1, 2].transAxes, 
                fontsize=11, verticalalignment='top', fontfamily='monospace',
                bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='lightblue', alpha=0.8))

axes[1, 2].text(0.1, 0.35, result_text, transform=axes[1, 2].transAxes, 
                fontsize=12, verticalalignment='top', fontweight='bold',
                bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor=color, alpha=0.8))

Comments

  • Time Plot
    • Except for the occasional spikes, the time plot seems to be mostly random noise.
    • Hence, residuals are mostly white noise.
  • Normality
    • Distribution plot: The distribution is centered around zero. The distribution is also more peaked compared to normal and negatively skewed (aligns with calcuated skewness).
    • q-q plot: Normality seems acceptable if outliers are excluded.
    • Shapiro-Wilk test: Not normal.
    • Kurtosis: Indicates heavily tailednes, but I think this is due to the few outliers.
  • Conclusion
    • The failure of the Shapiro-Wilk test and the non-normality of other indicators are most likely due to the presence of outliers.

Comments

  • ACF and PACF
    • ACF and PACF plots indicate that there is no signal in the residuals when considered in isolation.
    • This suggests that the residuals are white noise.
  • Ljung-Box Test
    • Ljung-Box test indicates that there is no signal in the residuals jointly.
    • This suggests that the residuals are white noise.
  • Conclusion
    • Residuals are white noise.

Comments

  • There is no issue with the time plot and residuals are white noise/
  • However, residuals do not follow normal distribution despite being centered around zero.
  • Hypothesis: The failure of normality is most likely due to the presence of outliers.

Next Steps

  • Remove the residual outliers and repeat the residuals analysis.
  • Outliers would be detected using the 1.5*IQR method.

Residual Analysis Post-Outlier Removal using IQR bound¶

In [15]:
residuals_array = np.array(residuals)

# IQR Method
Q1 = np.percentile(residuals_array, 25)
Q3 = np.percentile(residuals_array, 75)
IQR = Q3 - Q1
lower_bound = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
upper_bound = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
outliers = np.where((residuals_array < lower_bound) | (residuals_array > upper_bound))[0]

print(f"Outliers detected: {len(outliers)}")

Outliers detected: 11

mu, std = residuals_no_outliers.mean(), residuals_no_outliers.std()
xmin, xmax = axes[0, 0].get_xlim()
x = np.linspace(xmin, xmax, 100)
p = norm.pdf(x, mu, std)
axes[0, 0].plot(x, p, 'r-', linewidth=2, label=f'Normal(μ={mu:.3f}, σ={std:.3f})')

axes[0, 0].set_ylabel('Density')

axes[0, 1].grid(True, alpha=0.3)
# Plot 3: Distribution plot comparison (Before vs After)

axes[1, 0].hist(residuals_no_outliers, bins=50, edgecolor='black', alpha=0.7, density=True, label='Without outliers', color='blue')
axes[1, 0].axvline(x=0, color='black', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)

  • Skewness is low and the distribution shape looks symmetric. Therefore, skewness is acceptable.

    • Therefore, AR(2) is not needed and the more parsimonious model, AR(1) is preferred.
  • Comparison with ARMA(1,1)
    • AR coefficient and intercept are very different.
    • Additionally, AR(1) was chosen after giving up an MA(1) model.
    • Considering both of these, an ARIMA(1,1,1) would be trained next.

    • Robust Estimation

Determining best ARIMA(1,1,1) model parameter estimation method¶

In [20]:
# Method 1: Standard MLE
arima_standard = ARIMA(distance_from_center, order=(1, 1, 1)).fit()

# Method 2: Robust estimation (Hannan-Rissanen)
arima_robust = ARIMA(distance_from_center, order=(1, 1, 1)).fit(method='hannan_rissanen')

diff_actual = np.diff(distance_from_center)

resid_standard = arima_standard.resid[1:]
resid_robust = arima_robust.resid[1:]

fitted_diff_standard = diff_actual - resid_standard
fitted_diff_robust = diff_actual - resid_robust

print("\n" + "="*80)
print("MODEL COMPARISON - AIC")
print("="*80)
print(f"\n1. ARIMA(1,1,1) Default:")
print(f"   AIC: {arima_standard.aic:.4f}")
print(f"\n2. ARIMA(1,1,1) Robust (Hannan-Rissanen):")
print(f"   AIC: {arima_robust.aic:.4f}")

print("="*80)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(18, 6))

Conclusion: AR(1) is best ARIMA(p,d,q) model in modelling simple cat sketches.¶

Finding Optimal VARIMA hyperparameters using grid search¶

In [22]:
x = seq[:, 1]
y = seq[:, 2]

# Combine data
data_2d = pd.DataFrame({
    'x': x,
    'y': y
})

print("\n" + "="*80)
print("VARMAX AUTO MODEL SELECTION")
print("="*80)

# STEP 1: Auto-determine differencing order (d) using augmented Dickey-Fuller tests
print("\nSTEP 1: Determining differencing order (d)...")
print("-"*80)

def determine_d(series, max_d=2):
    for d in range(max_d + 1):
        if d == 0:
            test_series = series
        else:
            test_series = series.diff(d).dropna()
        
        adf_stat, adf_pval = adfuller(test_series)[:2]
        
        print(f"  d={d}: ADF p-value = {adf_pval:.4f}", end="")
        if adf_pval < 0.05:
            print(" ✅ STATIONARY")
            return d, test_series
        else:
            print(" ❌ Non-stationary")
    
    return max_d, series.diff(max_d).dropna()

# Check for each series
print("x:")
d_x, _ = determine_d(data_2d['x'])
print("y:")
d_y, _ = determine_d(data_2d['y'])

# Use maximum d
d_order = max(d_x, d_y)
print(f"\n✅ Selected d = {d_order}")

# Apply differencing
if d_order > 0:
    data_diff = data_2d.diff(d_order).dropna()
    print(f"   Applied {d_order} order differencing")
else:
    data_diff = data_2d
    print("   No differencing needed")

# STEP 2: Grid search for p and q using AIC
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("STEP 2: Grid search for optimal (p, q)...")
print("-"*80)

p_range = range(0, 4)  # Adjust if needed
q_range = range(0, 4)

best_aic = np.inf
best_order_aic = None
best_model_aic = None

results_list = []

total_combinations = (len(p_range) * len(q_range)) - 1  # -1 for (0,0)
current = 0

print(f"\nTesting {total_combinations} model combinations...\n")

for p, q in itertools.product(p_range, q_range):
    if p == 0 and q == 0:
        continue
    
    current += 1
    
    try:
        model = VARMAX(data_diff, order=(p, q), trend='c')
        fitted = model.fit(disp=False, maxiter=1000)
        
        aic = fitted.aic
        
        results_list.append({
            'p': p,
            'd': d_order,
            'q': q,
            'AIC': aic,
            'Converged': True
        })
        
        print(f"  [{current:2d}/{total_combinations}] VARMAX({p},{d_order},{q}): AIC={aic:8.2f}")
        
        # Track best by AIC
        if aic < best_aic:
            best_aic = aic
            best_order_aic = (p, d_order, q)
            best_model_aic = fitted
            
    except Exception as e: # Error handling to prevent loss of results
        print(f"  [{current:2d}/{total_combinations}] VARMAX({p},{d_order},{q}): FAILED")
        results_list.append({
            'p': p,
            'd': d_order,
            'q': q,
            'AIC': np.nan,
            'Converged': False
        })

# STEP 3: Display results
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("🏆 BEST MODELS")
print("="*80)
print(f"\nBy AIC: VARMAX{best_order_aic}")
print(f"  AIC = {best_aic:.4f}")

# Show comparison table
results_df = pd.DataFrame(results_list)
results_df_converged = results_df[results_df['Converged'] == True].copy()

print("\n" + "="*80)
print("ALL SUCCESSFUL MODELS (sorted by AIC)")
print("="*80)
print(results_df_converged.sort_values('AIC').to_string(index=False))

# Use best model by AIC
best_model = best_model_aic
best_order = best_order_aic

print("\n" + "="*80)
print(f"✅ SELECTED MODEL: VARMAX{best_order}")
print("="*80)
print(best_model.summary())

# Store for later use
varmax_final = best_model
varmax_order = best_order
varmax_resid = best_model.resid

print("\n" + "="*80)
print("✅ MODEL SELECTION COMPLETE!")
print(f"   Final model: VARMAX{varmax_order}")
print(f"   AIC: {best_model.aic:.4f}")
print("="*80)

Analysing VARIMA’s ability in drawing a cat¶

In [23]:
# Rolling Origin with Increasing Horizon forecasting - FIT AT EACH POINT AND FORECAST H (increases with each iteration) STEPS AHEAD
# Cat will be sketched using the H-th step only
# Many cats will be drawn for different H and the quality degradation will be analyzed

print("\n" + "="*80)
print("🐱 Rolling Origin with Increasing Horizon forecasting - BUILD CAT FROM H-STEP FORECASTS".upper())
print("="*80)

MAX_FORECAST_HORIZON = [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100]  # maximum forecast horizon
max_steps = max(MAX_FORECAST_HORIZON) # The furthest we ever need to look ahead
min_horizon = min(MAX_FORECAST_HORIZON) # The latest we can possibly start stopping

p, d, q = varmax_order  # From best model

print(f"\nConfiguration:")
print(f"  Model order: VARMAX({p}, {d}, {q})")
print(f"  Maximum forecast horizon: {MAX_FORECAST_HORIZON}")
print(f"  Total actual data points: {len(data_2d)}")

data_2d_float = data_2d[['x', 'y']].astype(float).copy() # fix VARMAX data type issue

forecast_storage = {h: [] for h in MAX_FORECAST_HORIZON}

success_count = 0
fail_count = 0

print(f"\n{'='*80}")
print(f"🔮 Processing Rolling Origin Forecasts (Max Horizon: {max_steps})")
print(f"{'='*80}")

# Loop until the end of data minus the smallest horizon. 
# Larger horizons will simply stop collecting data earlier within the loop.
loop_end = len(data_2d_float) - min_horizon

for i in range(p+d+1, loop_end):
    
    train_data = data_2d_float.iloc[:i+1].copy()
    
    try:
        model = VARMAX(train_data, order=(p, q), trend='c')
        model_fit = model.fit(disp=False, maxiter=500, warn_convergence=False)
        
        forecast = model_fit.forecast(steps=max_steps)
        
        # Distribute the forecast steps to their respective horizon buckets
        for h in MAX_FORECAST_HORIZON:
            # Edge Case
            if i + h < len(data_2d_float):
                
                forecasted_x = forecast.iloc[h-1, 0]
                forecasted_y = forecast.iloc[h-1, 1]
                
                forecast_storage[h].append({
                    'original_index': i + h,
                    'x': forecasted_x,
                    'y': forecasted_y
                })
        
        success_count += 1
        
        if (i + 1) % 20 == 0:
             print(f"  Progress: {i+1}/{loop_end} | Fits: {success_count} | Fails: {fail_count}", end='\r')

    except Exception as e: 
        fail_count += 1
        if fail_count <= 3: 
            print(f"\n  ⚠️ Model fit failed at i={i} (train size={len(train_data)}): {str(e)[:80]}")
        continue

# Convert lists to DataFrames
all_forecasted_cats = {}
for h in MAX_FORECAST_HORIZON:
    all_forecasted_cats[h] = pd.DataFrame(forecast_storage[h])
    print(f"\nHorizon {h}: Generated {len(all_forecasted_cats[h])} points")

print(f"\nTotal Fits: {success_count}, Total Failed Fits: {fail_count}")

print("\n" + "="*80)

n_rows = int(np.ceil(len(MAX_FORECAST_HORIZON) / n_cols))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(6*n_cols, 5*n_rows))
axes = axes.flatten() if len(MAX_FORECAST_HORIZON) > 1 else [axes]

for idx, (horizon, forecast_df) in enumerate(all_forecasted_cats.items()):
    ax = axes[idx]
        
    # Forecasted plot
    if len(forecast_df) > 0:
        ax.scatter(forecast_df['x'], forecast_df['y'], c='red', s=20, alpha=0.6)
    
    # Mark start
    ax.plot(data_2d.iloc[0]['x'], data_2d.iloc[0]['y'],
            'o', color='green', markersize=12, label='Start', zorder=5)
    
    ax.set_xlabel('X', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_ylabel('Y', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_title(f'Horizon {horizon}: Cat from {horizon}-Step Forecasts', 
                fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(loc='best', fontsize=9)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3, linestyle='--')
    ax.set_aspect('equal', adjustable='box')
    ax.set_ylim(50, 450)
    ax.set_xlim(400, 800)
    ax.invert_xaxis()
    ax.invert_yaxis()

# Hide extra subplots
for idx in range(len(MAX_FORECAST_HORIZON), len(axes)):
    axes[idx].set_visible(False)

plt.suptitle(f'Cat Trajectory Decay - VARMAX({p},{q})', 
                fontsize=18, fontweight='bold', y=1.00)

Comments

  • As the number of forecast steps increases:
    • The cat degrades.
    • The cat rotates away.
    • The cat's lower half disappears.
  • This shows that VARIMA learns some ability to sketch a cat when rolling origin with increasing horizon forecasting is used.
  • However, this ability degrades quickly as the forecast steps increase.
